title: Gerunds vs Infinitives vs Participles — Clear Rules for SSC CGL & Bank PO
excerpt: Most students mix gerunds, infinitives and participles because textbooks treat them as three separate lists. This post shows the exact decision system that stops the confusion and helps you pick the right form under exam pressure.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Three forms. One verb. Endless confusion. Gerunds, infinitives and participles quietly cost SSC CGL and Bank PO aspirants marks every year because most students learn them as three separate lists instead of one clear decision system. Once you see which form the sentence actually needs, the guessing stops.

Quick Answer: A gerund is the -ing form used as a noun (Swimming is good). An infinitive is to + base verb used as noun, adjective or adverb (I want to swim). A participle is the -ing or -ed form used as an adjective or to form continuous/perfect tenses (The swimming boy / The broken chair).

Why Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles Feel Harder Than They Are

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students do not struggle with the names. Almost everyone can say "gerund ends with -ing". What breaks down is choosing the right form when the sentence gives no clear signal, or when two forms look possible.

  • You know the definitions but freeze when a verb can take both gerund and infinitive with different meanings.
  • You use "to + verb" everywhere because it feels safer, even when the gerund is required.
  • You confuse the present participle (adjective or continuous tense) with the gerund (noun).
  • You have never seen one simple decision order that works for almost every exam question.
  • I know exactly how that feels — I watched this same mix-up cost students marks for years before I started teaching the forms as one decision tree instead of three lists.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorise long lists of verbs that take gerunds or infinitives, instead of learning the purpose each form serves in the sentence.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Using infinitive after verbs that only take gerunds.
Verbs like enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep and practise are followed by the gerund, not the infinitive. Students often add "to" out of habit and lose easy marks.

2. Treating every -ing word as a gerund.
The -ing form can be a gerund (noun) or a present participle (adjective or part of continuous tense). Mixing the two leads to wrong sentence correction answers.

3. Ignoring meaning change with verbs that take both forms.
Verbs like stop, remember, forget and try change meaning depending on whether a gerund or infinitive follows. Examiners love these traps.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Infinitive after gerund-only verbs

Enjoy, finish, avoid, mind and keep take only the gerund.

Wrong: She enjoys to read novels.

Correct: She enjoys reading novels.

❌
Mistake 2: Calling every -ing form a gerund

If the -ing word describes a noun, it is a participle, not a gerund.

Wrong: The running man is a gerund.

Correct: The running man — "running" is a present participle.

❌
Mistake 3: Ignoring meaning change

Stop + gerund and stop + infinitive mean different things.

Wrong: He stopped to smoke (when you mean he quit the habit).

Correct: He stopped smoking (he quit the habit).

The Complete Decision System, Step by Step

Stop memorising long lists. Use this fixed order every time you see a verb form choice in an exam question.

FormMain JobQuick Test
Gerund (-ing)Acts as a nounCan I replace it with "something"?
Infinitive (to + verb)Noun, adjective or adverbDoes it show purpose, intention or result?
Present Participle (-ing)Adjective or continuous tenseDoes it describe a noun or form a tense?
Past Participle (-ed/-en)Adjective or perfect/passiveDoes it describe a finished state?

Step 1: Ask what job the word is doing in the sentence. If it is the subject or object, you almost always need a gerund.

❌ To swim is good for health.
✅ Swimming is good for health. (subject of the sentence needs a gerund)

Step 2: Check the verb that comes before the form. Some verbs take only gerunds, some take only infinitives, and a few take both with a meaning change.

❌ She finished to write the letter.
✅ She finished writing the letter. (finish takes only gerund)

Step 3: Watch the meaning-change verbs. Stop, remember, forget, try, regret and go on change meaning with gerund vs infinitive. Learn the difference once and the trap disappears.

Step 4: Separate participle from gerund by asking one question. Is the -ing word naming an activity (gerund) or describing a noun (participle)?

❌ I saw the crying of the child. (wrong use)
✅ I saw the crying child. (participle describing child)

Step 5: Use infinitive of purpose when the sentence shows why someone does something. "I went to the market to buy vegetables" is purpose, so infinitive is correct.

Step 6: Practise the high-frequency pairs that appear in almost every paper. enjoy + gerund, want + infinitive, stop + gerund/infinitive, remember + gerund/infinitive, look forward to + gerund.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Ask what job the word does

Subject or object → gerund. Purpose → infinitive.

Example: Swimming keeps me fit.

2
Check the verb before the form

Enjoy, finish, avoid → gerund only.

Example: She avoided meeting him.

3
Learn the meaning-change list

Stop, remember, forget, try change meaning with the form.

4
Separate participle from gerund

Describes a noun → participle. Names an activity → gerund.

Example: the sleeping child (participle)

5
Use infinitive for purpose

When the sentence answers "why", choose the infinitive.

6
Drill the high-frequency pairs

look forward to + gerund, want + infinitive, keep + gerund.

A Quick Turnaround Story

One of my Bank PO students kept choosing the infinitive in almost every question. She said "to + verb" felt safer. We spent three days only on the decision order: first ask the job of the word, then check the verb before it, then check for meaning change. In the next mock she got every gerund-infinitive question right. The only thing that changed was the order she used to look at the sentence. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From the Classroom

  • Always ask "What job is this word doing?" first. Subject or object almost always needs a gerund.
  • Make a small personal list of the ten most common gerund-only verbs. Enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise, delay, consider, suggest, miss.
  • Treat stop, remember, forget and try as special cases. Write one example for each meaning and revise them before every mock.
  • Never decide by sound. Spoken English often mixes the forms; exam English follows the rules strictly.

The Bottom Line

Gerunds, infinitives and participles stop being confusing the moment you stop treating them as three separate lists and start using one decision order: job of the word, verb before it, meaning change, then participle check. Master that sequence and this topic becomes a steady source of marks.

Practice Questions (Exam Pattern Drills)

Q1 (SSC CGL Exam Pattern): She is interested in _____ (learn) new languages.

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: learning

Explanation: After the preposition "in" we need a gerund (Step 1 and Step 2). "Interested in" is always followed by the -ing form.

Q2 (Bank PO Exam Pattern): He stopped _____ (smoke) last year and now feels much better.

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: smoking

Explanation: "Stopped smoking" means he quit the habit. "Stopped to smoke" would mean he paused another activity in order to smoke (Mistake 3 and Step 3).

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. What is the main difference between a gerund and a present participle?
A gerund acts as a noun (Swimming is fun). A present participle acts as an adjective or helps form continuous tenses (the swimming boy / He is swimming).
Q2. Which verbs are always followed by a gerund?
Common ones are enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise, delay, consider, suggest, miss, and look forward to.
Q3. Can the same verb take both gerund and infinitive?
Yes. Verbs like stop, remember, forget, try and regret take both forms but the meaning changes. You must learn both meanings.
Q4. Is "to" always part of the infinitive?
In most exam questions yes, but after certain verbs (make, let, help, modal verbs) we use the bare infinitive without "to".
Q5. How should I practise this topic for SSC CGL and Bank PO?
Focus on error-spotting and sentence-improvement questions that mix the three forms. Practise the meaning-change verbs every day for one week.
